To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have introduced a new method, called the p-filter, which controls FDR and group FDR simultaneously at any number of layers of partitioning of the hypotheses, under standard assumptions on the dependence between the hypotheses, and that the method is computationally efficient.

1) the p-filter procedure controls FDR at the level of individual hypotheses, and also controls FDR for user-specified groupings of hypotheses; 2) the procedure can be extended to multiple partitions, even when they are nonhierarchical; 3) the procedure is computationally efficient, and is implemented in R; 4) we provide a simulation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of the p-filter procedure.

the p-filter procedure controls both individual and group FDR simultaneously across multiple partitions, and that this procedure can be used in any setting where the hypotheses can be arranged in a tree, with the root being the entire set of hypotheses, and each branch being a subset of hypotheses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of controlling multiple testing procedures at multiple layers.
the development of methods that can control the FDR simultaneously for individual hypotheses as well as for user-specified groupings of these hypotheses, and can handle multiple such groupings.
the following question: how should one perform multiple hypothesis testing when the null hypotheses can be naturally arranged into multiple groups?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the p-filter can simultaneously control the FDR and group FDR for multiple partitions of hypotheses under a nonnegative dependence assumption.
the p-filter can be viewed as a multi-level generalization of both the FDR and global null testing procedures.

the p-filter can simultaneously control the FDR at the most fine-grained level of individual hypotheses, as well as the FDR at any coarser level of user-specified partitions of the hypotheses (even if these are nonhierarchical partitions), and the FDR at even more coarser levels (e.g., if the user specifies multiple partitions).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we introduce a new method for FDR that controls the number of false positives at the finest level and also controls the number of falsely rejected groups at coarser levels, and that can handle multiple non-hierarchical partitions of the hypotheses.

we propose a new procedure for FDR control, the p-filter, and prove that it can control FDR simultaneously at multiple levels, including the individual hypothesis level, and at multiple partitions of the hypotheses, which are not necessarily hierarchical.
the p-filter procedure can control the FDR across multiple layers of hypotheses (e.g. hypotheses grouped by time and location), and can also handle multiple partitions which may be nonhierarchical.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the standard Benjamini–Hoch- berg FDR procedure can be generalized to simultaneously control FDR at the individual level and at the group level.
the standard FDR method can be extended to handle more complex situations, and can be applied to problems that were previously not amenable to the FDR approach.

we provide a simple procedure which controls the FDR at multiple layers of hypotheses, and we do not need to make any additional assumptions about the data beyond those that have been studied in the literature.
